questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Why A Shallow Copy Can Still Reach Back
questions.learningObjective: explain how a shallow copy leaves the original reachable through nested values
questions.stem: A program takes a shallow copy of a nested list, changes a value inside one of the inner lists, and is surprised to find the original changed too. Explain why the copy did not protect the original, and what a shallow copy actually guarantees.

answer.exemplar: A shallow copy duplicates one level, and one level is not the same as a whole object graph. The new outer list gets its own slots, so adding or removing an item from the outer list is invisible to the original, but the slots it copies hold the same references to the same inner lists, so the first change made through either name lands in the shared inner list. That is the whole guarantee: the top container is independent, everything it points at is not. The belief that a copy means a snapshot is what makes the surprise feel like a defect in the language rather than a documented limit of the operation. The fix depends on intent. If the program only ever adds to the outer container, the shallow copy is enough and cheaper, because it duplicates one object instead of the whole tree. If any inner value can be written, a deep copy is required, and the cost is proportional to the number of objects reachable from the top. Where the nesting is shallow and fixed, a program can also replace the inner lists with fresh ones explicitly, which duplicates only what it knows will change. A third option is to stop mutating in place and build a new structure instead, since a function that returns a new value never surprises its caller.

questions.explanation: A shallow copy duplicates the top container only, so the values that container points at are still shared and a write inside one of them reaches the original. The tempting defence is that copying should be a snapshot, which is exactly the belief the operation's name encourages and its documentation contradicts. The useful rule is to ask how deep the program writes, and to reach for a deep copy or a new-structure return only when that depth is greater than one.
questions.hint: Count the levels of nesting the copy actually duplicates before it stops.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: What A Stable Sort Promises
questions.learningObjective: explain what a stable sort guarantees about items that compare equal
questions.stem: Two records share the value a sort is ordering by, and the sorted result is used to decide which record to keep. Explain what a stable sort guarantees here, and why relying on an unstable sort for that decision is a hidden dependency.

answer.exemplar: A stable sort preserves the relative order of items that compare equal, so two records with the same ordering value stay in the order the input had them and the choice between them is decided by whatever the code deliberately did before the sort, such as putting the newest record last. That makes the outcome reproducible from the program alone. An unstable sort is free to place equal items in any order, so the same input may yield a different winner on a different run, on a different build, or after an unrelated change inside the library, and the code that kept the first record may now keep the second. Nothing in the source changes when this happens, which is what makes the dependency hidden: the program looks deterministic and is not. The fix is not to trust a particular run but to remove the ambiguity. If the ordering value is not enough to decide, add it to the sort key so the comparison itself can never tie, for example by pairing the score with the record time. Then the result is determined by the data rather than by the sort's internal choices, and the guarantee holds under any implementation. Where the key must stay a single value, sorting on a key tuple is the usual way to express the tie-break, and it costs nothing at run time beyond the extra comparisons.

questions.explanation: A stable sort keeps equal items in their original relative order, so a decision based on which record comes first after sorting is decided by the input rather than by the implementation. The tempting defence is that any correct sort may reorder equal items, which is true and irrelevant, because the program then has a result that no line of its own source explains. Adding the deciding value to the key removes the tie instead of relying on which sort happens to be in use.
questions.hint: Ask what two items that compare equal are guaranteed to keep.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Why A Halving Search Is Allowed To Be Fast
questions.learningObjective: explain the precondition that makes halving search correct as well as quick
questions.stem: A halving search on an unordered list returns a not-found answer for a value that is plainly present, while on an ordered list the same routine is correct and quick. Explain what the routine is assuming, and why that assumption is worth stating out loud.

answer.exemplar: The routine is assuming the list is already in ascending order, and every step it takes depends on that. It looks at the middle value and compares the target with it, then discards half the remaining range on the strength of that one comparison. When the list is ordered, discarding the half on the wrong side of the middle cannot remove the target, so each step is safe and the range of candidates roughly halves, which is why the number of comparisons grows with the logarithm of the length rather than with the length itself. When the list is unordered, the comparison still succeeds mechanically and the routine still discards half the range, but the discarded half may be the only place the target was sitting, so the answer it returns says nothing about the data. The program is not broken in that case; it is answering a question about a list that meets a condition nobody checked. This is why the precondition belongs in the interface rather than in a comment. If the routine accepted only ordered input, the type of its argument could say so and every caller would be forced to sort first, which costs a pass and makes the saving visible rather than hidden. Where the input cannot be ordered, a set answers membership in constant time and a plain sweep with a set gives the same result in one pass, so a halving search is worth reaching for exactly when the list is already ordered and the queries are many. A routine that silently assumes ordering is not faster, it is just unpredictable: it returns right answers until the day it does not, and the day it does not has no pattern a reader can see.

questions.explanation: Every halving step discards half the candidates on the strength of one comparison with the middle, and that is only sound when the list is ordered, so an unordered input makes the routine discard the target and report a not-found answer that is simply false. The tempting defence is that the routine is fast regardless, which is true in the sense that it still examines few positions and wrong in the sense that speed on a broken precondition buys nothing. Stating the requirement in the interface forces the caller to sort, which makes the cost visible and the saving real.
questions.hint: Ask why the routine is allowed to throw half the candidates away.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: What A Memo Table Removes
questions.learningObjective: explain what memoisation saves and what it charges for the saving
questions.stem: A naive recursive routine re-derives the same sub-results many times, and a memo table is added without changing the rule it follows. Explain what the table actually removes from the work, and what it costs to keep it.

answer.exemplar: The memo table removes repeated derivation, not repeated structure. A naive routine for a sequence such as the ones built from the two preceding values computes the same sub-result many times over, because every path down the recursion reaches the same value, and the total work grows exponentially in the requested index even though the number of distinct sub-results grows only linearly. The table makes each distinct sub-result be computed once, on its first arrival, and every later arrival is a single lookup, so the work collapses from exponential to linear in the number of distinct sub-results. The rule the routine follows has not changed at all, which is the point: the table is a cache of answers, not a new way of working them out. The cost has three parts and all of them are real. Memory grows with the number of distinct sub-results, so a routine whose sub-results are themselves large structures can use a great deal of it. Each call pays for a hash lookup and a store, and for small sub-results that overhead can exceed the arithmetic it saves. The cache is state that lives between calls, so a routine that caches into a table shared across callers needs a rule about when that table is cleared, or a stale entry from an earlier run will be returned as though it were current. It also makes the routine harder to follow, because the reader has to reason about which sub-results are already known, and that reasoning is exactly what the plain recursive version is legible about. Where the repeated work is small or the sub-results are few, the naive version is the better one, and the table is not worth its complexity. The rule of thumb is that memoisation pays when the same expensive question is asked many times over many different paths and the answer is a small value that can be keyed cheaply.

questions.explanation: The table stores each distinct sub-result the first time it is derived, so later arrivals are a lookup instead of a fresh derivation, and the total work drops from growing with the paths to growing with the distinct results. The tempting claim that the table changes the routine is wrong, because the rule for computing a sub-result is untouched and only the number of times it is applied changes. What is charged for the saving is memory for the stored results, a hash operation on every call, and a cache that becomes state that must be invalidated when the inputs change.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rule for producing a sub-result changed, and what the table holds.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Why A Traversal Needs A Visited Table
questions.learningObjective: explain what a visited set prevents in a cyclic graph
questions.stem: A graph contains a link back to a node the walk has already reached, and a traversal written without any record of where it has been fails to finish. Explain what the missing record is for, and why the walk does not notice the loop by itself.

answer.exemplar: The missing record is the set of nodes already reached, and it exists because a graph with a link back to a node the walk has already seen has no natural stopping point. The walk's rule is local: it stands on a node and moves to its neighbours, and it has no way to tell a neighbour that leads somewhere new from one that leads back along the path it arrived by, because both are simply names in a list. Every time it revisits the earlier node it will follow that node's neighbours again, which brings it back to the same node, which follows the same neighbours again, and the process never produces anything new while never terminating. It does not notice because nothing in the data is marked as already visited: a node's neighbour list is the same whether it was reached once or fifty times, and the graph is not changed by being walked. The visited set changes the walk rather than the graph, and it is checked at exactly the point where a node is about to be accepted, so the first arrival is recorded and every later arrival is refused. That check is what converts an open-ended walk into one whose length is bounded by the number of nodes, and it is also what makes the walk terminate on a graph that has no cycle at all, where the same check simply never fires. A cheaper variant checks membership in the growing output list rather than maintaining a separate set, which costs a linear scan per test instead of a constant one and is usually not worth it once the graph is more than a handful of nodes. Where a graph is known to be acyclic in advance, the check can be omitted, and omitting it in the general case is the mistake this pattern exists to prevent.

questions.explanation: The walk's rule is local, so nothing in the data distinguishes a neighbour that leads somewhere new from one that leads back along the path already taken, and a cyclic graph therefore offers a route that never reaches anything and never ends. The visited set is checked where a node is about to be accepted, so the first arrival is recorded and every later one is refused, which bounds the walk by the number of nodes. The tempting claim that the loop is self-evidently visible to the walk is wrong, because a node's neighbour list is identical whether it has been reached once or many times.
questions.hint: Ask how the walk could tell a fresh neighbour from one it already reached.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: What A Set Does About Order
questions.learningObjective: explain why reading a set in order requires an extra step
questions.stem: A program stores its options in a set for quick membership tests and then prints them one per line, and the output order changes between runs of a program that was not changed. Explain what a set withholds, why printing a set depends on that, and what the program should do instead.

answer.exemplar: A set withholds an order, and it withholds it on purpose because the quick membership test is built on a hashed layout whose positions are chosen for lookup speed rather than for sequence, and the layout is free to change between runs and between versions. Printing a set hands those positions to the reader, so the output order is a property of that layout rather than a property of the data, which is exactly why a program that was not edited can print in a different order tomorrow. The tempting response is to read the order off one run and treat it as the order, which is the same mistake as writing a test against the current output. The program should state the order it intends. For alphabetical order the values are handed to the call that sorts them, and for the order the program established when it collected them the answer is to keep a list alongside the set, since the set answers whether an option is present and the list preserves where it came from. A third option, which is often the right one, is to decide that the order does not matter and make the consumer order-independent rather than fighting for a sequence that the structure never promised. What should not happen is relying on the incidental order: it produces output that differs across runs, snapshots that do not match, and a bug report that cannot be reproduced because the thing that changed is not in the code. If the order is genuinely load-bearing, it has to be written down in the code, and if it is not, the code should say so by not printing order at all.

questions.explanation: A set promises fast membership and distinctness, and it deliberately promises nothing about sequence, so printing one hands the reader a layout that was chosen for lookup speed and may change between runs or versions. The tempting defence is that the order looked sensible on one run, which is the same error as writing a test against whatever a structure happened to produce. The program should say which order it means, by sorting at the point of printing or by keeping a list alongside the set when the collection order is the intended one.
questions.hint: Ask which question a set was built to answer, and what it declines to answer.
